newsitem.title: JAPAN: ATM boom buoys profits at Japan personal loan firm.
newsitem.headline: ATM boom buoys profits at Japan personal loan firm.

text.p: One of Japan's leading consumer credit companies, Acom Co Ltd, reported a 20 percent rise in its interim profits on Tuesday, citing growing demand for discreet loans dispensed by cash machines.

The firm has a growing chain of automatic teller machines (ATMs) close to shops and railway stations from which customers can borrow funds in the same way that they would draw out money from a bank account.

In a nation where cash is still often preferred over credit cards, the machines have proved popular with consumers as a discreet way of financing purchases by credit but actually paying the bill in cash.

"In our loan sector, we increased the number of our automatic teller machines (ATMs), built more roadside outlets and expanded our cash dispenser network by establishing ties with other financial institutions," Acom said in a statement.
The firm said its parent current profit was 42.42 billion yen ($372 million) in the six months to September 30 against 35.41 billion yen ($310 million) in the year-ago period.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses and gains on non-operating activities such as investments in shares.

The firm also expects to enjoy buoyant profits for the full business year ending next March, predicting a parent current profit of 83.80 billion yen ($735 million) against 75.54 billion yen ($662 million) a year earlier, which would be a rise of 11 percent.
A company spokeswoman said that in the half year, the firm installed 294 new ATMs across Japan, bringing its total to 645.

As a result, the firm, which is in its 60th year of business, increased its outstanding loans by 17.5 percent to 918.99 billion yen ($8.06 billion) compared with the same half-year period a year earlier. Interest income on the loans stood at 114.97 billion yen ($1 billion), up 14.7 percent.
Analysts said the key to the clientele expansion at the consumer credit firms, once frowned upon as loan sharks charging outrageously high interest rates, lies in the increasing use of ATMs.

They added that despite the increase in borrowings, the firms were relatively safe from any damage from non-performing loans, as their loans are for individuals and not firms, and the sums are not staggering.
Many Japanese banks and loan institutions were badly burned by the lending boom of the late 1980s economic "bubble" era, which left them with large amounts of corporate bad loans.

Japan's record low interest rates, aimed at getting the sluggish economy back in high gear, are also a big plus for the consumer finance firms, which themselves borrow funds from financial institutions, industry sources said.
By the end of the current fiscal year, the company hopes to raise the number of its ATMs to 780.
Acom shares, which are listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange, settled 10 yen higher at 4,390 yen. ($1=114 yen)
